source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (U Colorado Law Rev 67)
finding: The authors restate the story model: coverage and coherence govern which story is accepted; uniqueness adds to confidence. Coverage is how much of the trial evidence the story accounts for. Poor coverage lowers confidence in the story and in the verdict.
quote: The greater the story's coverage, the more acceptable the story will be as an explanation of the evidence
limits: Verbal theory statement written after the O.J. trial; no new data in this passage.
agent_relevance: Coverage can be counted by code: share of evidence items that a candidate answer's account explains. Rank candidates by it.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (U Colorado Law Rev 67)
finding: Coherence has three parts: consistency (no internal contradiction with believed evidence or other story parts), plausibility (fits what typically happens in the world), completeness (the expected story structure has all its parts, with motives, plans and intentions linking episodes). The three combine into one coherence level.
numbers: Three components; no weights or formula given.
quote: A story is complete when the expected structure of the story has, in laymen's terms, 'all of its parts.'
limits: Components are not formally defined or measured separately here; the combination rule is not stated.
agent_relevance: Each part maps to a code check: contradiction scan (consistency), missing-slot count in a fixed template (completeness). Plausibility needs a model judge and is the weak part.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (U Colorado Law Rev 67)
finding: Uniqueness rule: if more than one story is judged coherent, the stories lack uniqueness and belief in any one of them is diminished. If there is a single coherent story, it is accepted. So uniqueness changes confidence, not which story is picked.
quote: If there are multiple coherent explanations for the available evidence, belief in any one of them over the others will necessarily be diminished.
limits: Stated as a principle; the 1996 text gives no number for how much confidence drops per extra coherent story.
agent_relevance: Direct design hook: confidence = f(number of rival answers that pass the same checks). Two passing rivals means report low confidence or ask for a discriminating test.

source: Hastie & Pennington (1996) The O.J. Simpson stories: behavioral scientists' reflections (U Colorado Law Rev 67)
finding: The certainty principles sit inside a three-stage model: build a story from evidence plus knowledge, learn verdict categories, match story to category. Coverage and coherence settle acceptance of one story; uniqueness only modulates confidence.
numbers: Two acceptance principles (coverage, coherence) plus one confidence principle (uniqueness).
limits: Founding experiments (1986, 1988, 1992) not opened this session; see a27-a29.
agent_relevance: Separates 'which candidate wins' (coverage, coherence) from 'how sure to be' (uniqueness). The schema can keep these two outputs apart.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12:435)
finding: Thagard states seven principles of explanatory coherence: symmetry, explanation, analogy, data priority, contradiction, acceptability, system coherence. Principle 2 (explanation) is the most important: a hypothesis coheres with what it explains, co-hypotheses cohere, and the more hypotheses needed, the lower the coherence. This is a formal cousin of coverage plus simplicity.
numbers: 7 principles; program ECHO applied to more than a dozen scientific and legal cases.
limits: Local text copy of the BBS target article; coherence is relative to the set of competing hypotheses supplied.
agent_relevance: Gives a computable definition of 'best explanation' in which breadth and parsimony enter as link weights. Usable as a scoring rule in code.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12:435)
finding: ECHO is a connectionist network. Propositions are units; explanation links are excitatory, contradiction and competition links are inhibitory; activation spreads in parallel until the network settles. Positive final activation means accept, negative means reject.
numbers: Defaults: data excitation .1, decay .05, inhibition -.2 (tolerance .25), simplicity impact 1, analogy impact 1. Author states results hold over a wide parameter range (sensitivity appendix).
limits: Links are hand-coded from the analyst's reading of the case; no learning. Commentators question the binary-hypothesis assumption.
agent_relevance: Constraint satisfaction over a graph of claims is implementable in plain code. It decides by settling, not by a model's opinion.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12:435)
finding: Thagard builds explicitly on Pennington and Hastie (1986, 1987) and runs ECHO on two real murder trials. In the Peyer trial the real jury hung (7 for conviction on second-degree murder, 5 against); ECHO found more coherence in the guilt hypotheses but rejected innocence much less strongly than it did in the Chambers case.
numbers: Peyer jury split 7 to 5; sensitivity Table 11 shows innocence rejected less strongly than in Chambers.
limits: Single-case fits from newspaper coverage, not a controlled test; no quantitative match to juror confidence.
agent_relevance: A weak rejection of the rival (not a clear win) tracks a split human jury. The margin between best and second-best could serve as a confidence signal.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence (Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12:435)
finding: Peer commentary in the same issue criticises the approach. One commentator notes Pennington and Hastie give no theory of what makes a good story, and that story-order effects conflict with Bayesian updating, which is order-free. Another doubts the system's meaning once it goes beyond the binary hypothesis.
limits: Commentary is opinion, not data.
agent_relevance: Order sensitivity separates story-style from probabilistic aggregation. Our agent should not let evidence order change a code-selected answer unless tested.

source: Thagard (2003) Why wasn't O.J. convicted? Emotional coherence in legal inference (Cognition and Emotion 17:361)
finding: Given the O.J. trial evidence, ECHO accepts that Simpson was the killer and that the LAPD tried to frame him, and rejects the drug-dealer alternative. So explanatory coherence alone predicts conviction, which the jury did not deliver. Cold coherence is not enough to predict the verdict.
numbers: ECHO finds Simpson guilty, even without the inadmissible fibre and Bruno Magli shoe evidence.
quote: ECHO, unlike the jury, finds Simpson guilty.
limits: One case, one author's coding of the network. Author admits jurors' networks could differ.
agent_relevance: Coherence maximising can pick the wrong winner when the network encodes what jurors do not share (priors, emotion). Code-picked coherence still needs outside checks (G3).

source: Thagard (2003) Why wasn't O.J. convicted? Emotional coherence in legal inference (Cognition and Emotion 17:361)
finding: A Bayesian network (JavaBayes) built on the same evidence also found guilt. It needed 60 conditional probabilities, several of them guesses. Thagard concludes the coherence network is simpler and more psychologically natural than the Bayes net, but neither explains the acquittal.
numbers: P(OJ killed Nicole | evidence)=.72; P(drug killings | evidence)=.29; P(LAPD framed | evidence)=.99 (author calls the last too high).
limits: Conditional probabilities were the author's guesses, so the .72 is not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Probability tables for narratives are costly and arbitrary; ranking by graph coherence in code is cheaper and gave the same direction here.

source: Thagard (2003) Why wasn't O.J. convicted? Emotional coherence in legal inference (Cognition and Emotion 17:361)
finding: Thagard adds valences (emotion) to ECHO as HOTCO: each unit has an activation and a valence, and valence feeds back into activation. A strongly positive valence on the accused suppresses acceptance of guilt. This is offered as the missing piece for the acquittal.
numbers: Activation update: a_j(t+1)=a_j(t)(1-d)+net_j(max-a_j(t)) if net_j>0, else net_j(a_j(t)-min); d about .05. Poll figures cited: 3% of 200 African-Americans assumed guilt.
limits: Model is fitted after the verdict; the poll data are context, not a predictive test.
agent_relevance: Value-laden inputs shift coherence outcomes. G4 and G5 (no authorship, no stated answer shown to the judge) keep valence out.

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction (J Exp Psychol: General 128:3)
finding: Founding experiment on coherence as a process. College students judged an ambiguous civil case (Quest v. Smith, internet libel) with six paired arguments, rated each argument alone before the case and again after a verdict. Ratings moved to agree with the verdict, so reasoning ran both ways: evidence to verdict and verdict back to evidence.
numbers: Experiment 1: 54 undergraduates; 48 analysed after dropping 6 switchers; verdicts 26 Quest, 22 Smith; 75% gave confidence 4 or 5 of 5. Verdict x test interaction F(1,44)=35.3 (MSE 22.6, p<.001) on Q-scores.
limits: One case, American students, paper ratings. Pretest ratings of the eventual groups were similar; posttest groups differed strongly.
agent_relevance: A chosen answer pulls the rated strength of its supporting facts. If the agent rates evidence after choosing, those ratings are contaminated. Rate evidence before choosing and log it.

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction (J Exp Psychol: General 128:3)
finding: Ambiguity plus high confidence: the verdict split was about even, yet most students were very confident. Constraint satisfaction predicts this, because one coherent set becomes highly active and inhibits the rival set. Confidence also rose from preliminary leaning to final verdict.
numbers: Confidence from leaning to final verdict rose, t(21)=5.02, p<.001 (3-phase group); interim M 3.36.
limits: Self-reported confidence; the case had no ground truth.
agent_relevance: Confidence after coherence building is inflated even when evidence splits half and half. Do not read the model's own certainty as a sign of correctness.

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction (J Exp Psychol: General 128:3)
finding: Experiment 2 (small replication, 1-week delay): the same divergence appeared after a week, and students' recall of their own pretest ratings moved toward their final verdict. The best predictor of the recalled score was the verdict, not the real pretest rating.
numbers: Verdict x test F(1,17)=7.71, p=.01; pretest Q-scores -.34 vs -.30; posttest .94 vs -1.03; verdict-recall r(16)=.43, p=.07.
limits: Small sample (about 19 analysed); the recall effect was only marginal (p=.07).
agent_relevance: The agent's record of earlier states must be kept outside its own text; a memory held in context will drift toward the final answer.

source: Holyoak & Simon (1999) Bidirectional reasoning in decision making by constraint satisfaction (J Exp Psychol: General 128:3)
finding: Experiment 3 manipulated the defendant's character (Bad vs Good Smith) and tracked spreading coherence. The character cue shifted verdicts and also the ratings of unrelated points. Coherence then carried to a second case that shared one analogy (newspaper vs telephone).
numbers: N=80 (32 per condition, 16 baseline). Motive Q-score 1.83 vs -2.75, t(62)=8.98; verdict for Quest 78% (Bad Smith) vs 28% (Good Smith), chi2(1,N=64)=16.1, p<.001. Other points: interaction F(1,62)=16.0.
limits: Transfer to the second case runs through one shared analogy; the transfer verdict effect size was not extracted here.
agent_relevance: One irrelevant cue can spread through a whole network of beliefs and into the next problem. Reset context between tasks to stop carry-over.

source: Simon, Pham, Le & Holyoak (2001) The emergence of coherence over the course of decision making (J Exp Psychol: LMC 27:1250)
finding: Experiment 1: coherence shifts appear before commitment. Students told to delay the decision and only give a preliminary leaning already showed the spread between rated arguments at the interim test. Whether leaning was asked before or after the ratings made no difference.
numbers: N=47 analysed (3 switchers dropped); verdicts 49% Quest, 51% Smith; 93% at least moderate confidence; interaction F(2,86)=35.3, MSE 27.9, p<.0001; leaning order F(2,86)<1. Quest-minus-Smith Q-score gap: .80 baseline, 2.23 interim, 2.55 postdecision.
limits: Interim-to-post shift not significant (p>.30), so most shift happens before the verdict. Baseline gap already significant (p=.01).
agent_relevance: Coherence builds while the agent is still deliberating, not only after answering. A pre-answer check of how rated facts line up with the leaning can detect early lock-in.

source: Simon, Pham, Le & Holyoak (2001) The emergence of coherence over the course of decision making (J Exp Psychol: LMC 27:1250)
finding: Experiment 2: coherence shifts also arise when students are only told to memorise the case, with no decision or judge role. Correlations among argument ratings went from near zero to strongly positive.
numbers: N=120 analysed of 125 (5 switchers); 56% Quest, 44% Smith; 88% moderate or higher confidence; F(2,236)=59.1, p<.0001. Cronbach alpha .08 (baseline), .70 (interim), .80 (postdecision); significant positive correlations among 21: 2 at baseline, all at postdecision.
limits: Baseline alpha near zero by design, since the arguments were unrelated at the start.
agent_relevance: Coherence building is automatic when processing complex text. Reading a long context can itself bias the model's later ratings.

source: Simon, Pham, Le & Holyoak (2001) The emergence of coherence over the course of decision making (J Exp Psychol: LMC 27:1250)
finding: Experiment 3: shifts occurred in all processing sets: decision, reception (read and wait for another student's account), communication (expect to explain it to someone). The pattern was statistically identical across the three conditions.
numbers: N=157 analysed of 166 (9 switchers); 58% Quest, 42% Smith; 91% moderate or higher confidence, 63% at 4-5. F(2,302)=78.6, p<.0001; condition x shift F(4,302)<1. Q-score gap .32 baseline, 2.03 interim, 2.50 post. Alpha .12, .77, .80.
limits: Switchers (about 5% of participants) were excluded, which may bias estimates.
agent_relevance: The authors read it as a general coherence-generating mechanism, not a decision-specific bias. An LLM may show the same effect inside any long reading task.

source: Simon, Pham, Le & Holyoak (2001) The emergence of coherence over the course of decision making (J Exp Psychol: LMC 27:1250)
finding: Across the three experiments the shift was large from baseline to the interim test and small after. The authors conclude coherence is generated while the case is processed, and decisions follow from it rather than the reverse.
quote: The findings support the hypothesis that a coherence-generating mechanism operates in a variety of processing tasks, including decision making.
limits: Correlational mediation; the shift itself was not manipulated. Dissonance accounts (post-decision) are argued against, not excluded in all settings.
agent_relevance: Supports locking the evidence ratings early and in code, because by the time the model writes a verdict they are already shifted.

source: Engel & Glockner (2013) Role-induced bias in court: an experimental analysis (J Behav Decis Making 26:272)
finding: Coherence shifts predict role-induced bias in legal judgment. Students assigned prosecutor or defence roles, then predicting the court ruling, still gave biased predictions even with a money incentive for accuracy. Bias came from devaluing evidence that conflicted with the favoured side.
numbers: Exp 1 (5 euro incentive): 149 students; predicted conviction 64% (prosecution, n=73) vs 50% (defence, n=76); subjective p(guilty) 66% vs 50%. Exp 2 (100 euro incentive): 56% vs 40% (n=50 vs 42); subjective p 65% vs 55%. Exp 3 (settlement): n=13 vs 16; 46% vs 37%.
quote: Role-induced bias is driven by coherence effects, that is, systematic information distortions in support of the favored option.
limits: Exp 3 had only 29 participants; a real criminal chamber supplied the benchmark ruling; the paper reports bias not removed by incentive or by the settlement frame.
agent_relevance: A role or persona in the prompt acts like an assigned side. Coherence distortion survives incentives for accuracy, so an accuracy instruction will not undo it (supports G4: no persona voters).

source: Engel & Glockner (2013) Role-induced bias in court: an experimental analysis (J Behav Decis Making 26:272)
finding: Coherence shifts were mostly confined to devaluing conflicting evidence. In Exp 1 the prosecution group lowered its valuation of contra-guilty evidence by 125 points while pro-guilty rose only 9.7; the defence group lowered pro-guilty by 54.5.
numbers: Coherence effect (pre to post), Exp 1: prosecution pro-guilty +9.7 (SE 10.2), contra-guilty -125.1 (SE 16.3); defence pro-guilty -54.5 (SE 16.6), contra-guilty -15.7 (SE 14.4).
limits: Scale units are the paper's own instrument; mediation used bootstrapped indirect effects.
agent_relevance: Distortion is mostly downweighting of disconfirming evidence. Critics should rate the disconfirming items first, before any answer is stated.

source: Dalal, Valentino, Freitas & Buitelaar (2024) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (ACL 2024)
finding: IBE-Eval scores candidate explanations on logical consistency (Prolog solver), parsimony (proof depth, concept drift), coherence (step-wise entailment) and linguistic uncertainty. On causal commonsense questions it picked the right explanation up to 77% of the time, 17.5% better on average than a GPT-3.5-as-judge baseline.
numbers: Tasks COPA (500 examples) and E-CARE; models GPT-3.5, Llama 2 13B and 7B. Table 1: GPT-3.5 judge .59 on the COPA GPT-3.5 column, human .95, best composed (consistency+depth+drift) .77.
quote: IBE-Eval can successfully identify the best explanation with up to 77% accuracy
limits: Two-option causal tasks only (chance 50%); explanations are model-generated; the authors note a tautology risk; some table cells sit near the random row.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of coherence-and-parsimony selection by code. A modest gain over a model judge; usable as a tie-breaker, not as a primary selector.

source: Dalal, Valentino, Freitas & Buitelaar (2024) Inference to the Best Explanation in Large Language Models (ACL 2024)
finding: Which criteria worked: parsimony (shorter proofs, less concept drift) was the most consistent predictor, with an average 14% improvement over consistency. Logical consistency gave little signal, because LLMs generate logically consistent explanations for any hypothesis, right or wrong.
numbers: Parsimony beat consistency by an average of 14% in the regression analysis; ablation in Table 1.
limits: Reading of the 14% comes from the text; the figure table was not re-derived.
agent_relevance: Consistency alone does not separate right from wrong when an LLM writes the explanation. Prefer coverage and parsimony counted in code, and check facts, not model-written arguments.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Mary, the Cheeseburger-Eating Vegetarian: Do LLMs Recognize Incoherence in Narratives? (arXiv 2512.07777)
finding: Hidden states of LLMs separate coherent from incoherent stories, but stated ratings do not. Probes at the incoherent sentence reach 80-96% accuracy; by the end of the story they fall toward chance for small models. Rating questions separate the stories only weakly.
numbers: Llama3.1-70B: probe at target .942, at end .817, perplexity .880, coherence response .765, quality rating .672. Qwen2.5-72B: .958, .817, .830, .707, .621. Llama3.1-8B: .850, .667, .880, .594, .595. No model separated quality ratings by more than one point except Llama-70B (1.66).
quote: LLMs generate responses to rating questions that fail to satisfactorily separate the coherent and incoherent narratives
limits: Short paired narratives adapted from human reading research; probing needs the location of the target sentence; reasoning models did not close the gap.
agent_relevance: The model knows internally about a contradiction but does not report it. Do not trust a model-written consistency judgement; use a probe or a code check on extracted claims.

source: de Langis et al. (2025) Mary, the Cheeseburger-Eating Vegetarian: Do LLMs Recognize Incoherence in Narratives? (arXiv 2512.07777)
finding: LLMs are more sensitive to incoherence from a setting violation (rain in the desert) than from a character violating a trait (a vegetarian ordering a cheeseburger). Human readers showed no such asymmetry.
numbers: Stimulus mix: 40% setting conflicts (n=10), 60% character conflicts; human contrast estimate 54.29, 95% CI [-117.39, 225.97], not significant.
limits: Small stimulus set; the human data were not designed to test story type.
agent_relevance: Plausibility checks by an LLM favour world-knowledge prototypes over story-internal consistency, so the plausibility part of coherence is the least reliable for the model.

source: Ersoz (2026) 12 Angry AI Agents: Evaluating multi-agent LLM decision-making through cinematic jury deliberation (arXiv 2605.01986)
finding: Twelve LLM juror agents debating the film's murder case almost never reach a verdict. They hold their starting vote and do not converge on one coherent story. The author calls anchoring the dominant failure mode.
numbers: 18 runs (2 models x 3 conditions x N=3): 17 hung juries, 1 NOT_GUILTY (Llama-4-Scout, no initial vote, 64 turns, 6 vote changes). GPT-4o mean 1.0 vote change per run; Llama-4-Scout 2.0 (baseline) to 6.0 (open-minded prompt).
limits: Exploratory, N=3 per cell, no significance tests, two models only, persona-conditioned agents.
agent_relevance: LLM groups do not do bidirectional coherence-building across agents. Outcomes follow starting positions, consistent with G4 (samples from one model are not independent).

source: Pennington & Hastie (1992) Explaining the evidence: tests of the story model for juror decision making (JPSP 62:189)
finding: Not opened: the APA page returned only 'Loading'. This is the main test of the story model. Only abstract-level claims known; no numbers were read from the paper this session.
numbers: No numbers read. Subfield 01 notes cite order-of-evidence cells of about 78% and 31% guilty verdicts, unverified and second-hand.
limits: Founding numbers remain second-hand. Do not quote 78% or 31% as verified.
agent_relevance: Treat founding effect sizes as unverified until the PDF is opened.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1988) Explanation-based decision making: effects of memory structure on judgment (JEP:LMC 14:521)
finding: Not opened (page returned 'Loading'). Cited by Thagard (1989) and the 1996 paper as the memory-structure test: whether evidence is given in story order or issue order changes verdicts.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Order sensitivity is a testable prediction for our agent; verify before use.

source: Pennington & Hastie (1993) Reasoning in explanation-based decision making (Cognition 49:123)
finding: Not opened (publisher redirect only). Cited by Thagard (2003) as the authors' generalisation of the story model from juries to explanation-based decision making.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Source of any general (non-legal) statement of coverage, coherence and uniqueness.

source: Simon & Holyoak (2002) Structural dynamics of cognition: from consistency theories to constraint satisfaction (Pers Soc Psychol Rev 6:283)
finding: Review placing coherence shifts in the history of consistency theories (balance, dissonance) and arguing that constraint satisfaction with bidirectional links explains legal coherence shifts. Three stated aims: show coherence can be reached under extreme ambiguity, show the pressure for coherence guides the decision rather than rationalising it, and show spreading coherence reaches remote inferences.
numbers: Summarises the Quest v. Smith series (Holyoak & Simon 1999; Simon et al. 2001) and a structural equation model of the character manipulation.
limits: Review; numbers repeat the primary papers. Only the legal-experiment section was read.
agent_relevance: Names three tests any coherence-based component should pass: works under ambiguity, acts before commitment, spreads to remote claims.
